steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our robotics paper on SG-Bot, an object rearrangement method that imagines goal scenes from scene graphs. Explain the task, the weaknesses of existing approaches, how SG-Bot works, and end with a list of contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Object rearrangement and its role in embodied AI
- Task definition and the three families of existing approaches, with their problems
- SG-Bot: observation, imagination, execution
- What makes SG-Bot different
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Object rearrangement
  - essential but challenging robot-environment interaction; crucial capability in embodied AI (cite)
  - automation via vision (cite), textual insights (cite), strategic motion planning (cite) -> sophisticated physical embodiment
- Task + existing approaches
  - robot starts from initial configuration, re-positions objects by rules/instructions, to reach goal states, using only sensory data + onboard perception
  - vision-based solutions, three types: known geometric/semantic goal states; sequential object pose estimation; zero-shot with large models
  - goal-guided (cite): quality of priors affects accuracy; unusable without goal state
  - pose estimation based (cite): sequential design fits manipulation but cumulative errors in autoregressive predictions
  - zero-shot (cite): commonsense in zero-shot models; need post-filter procedures or prompt templates; overlook scene-specific cues -> undesired outcomes
- SG-Bot
  - orthogonal; goal imagination on scene graphs + goal-guided object matching (Fig. 1)
  - three stages: observation, imagination, execution
  - observation: semantic instance segmentation to extract objects
  - imagination coarse-to-fine: objects as semantic nodes in goal scene graph, from commonsense reasoning or user-defined rules (coarse goal)
  - Graph-to-3D (cite) can decode graph to scene, but diverse results inconsistent with observation -> hurts matching
  - fix: shape priors -> shape-aware graph; finer imagination coherent with initial observation
  - execution: imagined objects as anchors for object matching by point cloud registration; occupancy check at each step for safe rearrangement
- Uniqueness
  - no known goal priors needed, self-generates goal scenes vs goal-required methods (cite)
  - per-object matching decouples transformation policy, less error accumulation vs autoregressive (cite)
  - concrete goals + closed-loop strategy guarantee performance vs loose-coupled zero-shot (cite)
- Contributions
  - SG-Bot new paradigm; coarse-to-fine goals from scene-graph rules; goal-guided matching = motion policies
  - shape priors from initial observation alleviate ambiguous goal generation -> better performance
  - simulation: competitive with SOTA; consistent in real world

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Object rearrangement is an essential but challenging task in the interaction between robots and the environment, and it is a crucial capability in embodied AI. This interactive ability reaches its highest level of automation by combining vision, textual insights from sources, and strategic motion planning. All these elements together give a sophisticated physical embodiment for robots.

Robotic rearrangement is the process where a robotic agent starts from an initial configuration in a scene and re-positions objects according to specific rules or instructions. The purpose is to reach desired goal states, and it only relies on sensory data and onboard perceptions. Recent vision-based solutions to this task can be put in three categories: using known geometric and semantic goal states, sequential object pose estimation, and zero-shot rearrangement with large models. For goal-guided methods, the quality of the priors usually affects the accuracy of the rearrangement a lot. If the goal state is not available, these methods cannot be used in the real world. Then, for approaches based on pose estimation, the sequential design fits well with robotic manipulations, but it can be affected by cumulative errors in the autoregressive predictions. The last type of methods use the commonsense knowledge stored in zero-shot models. They need either complicated post-filter procedures or prompt template designs, and these tend to overlook contextual cues specific to the scene and lead to diverse undesired outcomes.

- SG-Bot
  - orthogonal to the above; goal imagination on scene graphs + goal-guided object matching (Fig. 1)
  - three stages: observation, imagination, execution
  - observation: extract objects by semantic instance segmentation
  - imagination, coarse-to-fine: objects as semantic nodes in a constructed goal scene graph, directed by commonsense reasoning or user-defined rules = coarse goal
  - graph could be decoded with Graph-to-3D, but diverse results inconsistent with observation -> affects later matching
  - enrich graph with shape priors (shape-aware graph); finer imagination conditioned on it, coherent with initial observation
  - execution: imagined objects as anchors for object matching by point cloud registration; occupancy check each step
- Unique in three ways
  - no known goal priors, self-generates goal scenes (vs goal-required methods)
  - per-object matching, less error accumulation (vs autoregressive methods)
  - concrete goal states + closed loop guarantee performance (vs loose-coupled zero-shot methods)
- Contributions
  - SG-Bot new paradigm; coarse-to-fine goals from scene graph rules; goal-guided matching = motion policies
  - shape priors from initial observation -> less ambiguous goal generation, better performance
  - simulation: competitive with SOTA; consistent in real world

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Object rearrangement is an essential but challenging task in the interaction between robots and the environment, and it is a crucial capability in embodied AI. This interactive ability reaches its highest level of automation by combining vision, textual insights from sources, and strategic motion planning. All these elements together give a sophisticated physical embodiment for robots.

Robotic rearrangement is the process where a robotic agent starts from an initial configuration in a scene and re-positions objects according to specific rules or instructions. The purpose is to reach desired goal states, and it only relies on sensory data and onboard perceptions. Recent vision-based solutions to this task can be put in three categories: using known geometric and semantic goal states, sequential object pose estimation, and zero-shot rearrangement with large models. For goal-guided methods, the quality of the priors usually affects the accuracy of the rearrangement a lot. If the goal state is not available, these methods cannot be used in the real world. Then, for approaches based on pose estimation, the sequential design fits well with robotic manipulations, but it can be affected by cumulative errors in the autoregressive predictions. The last type of methods use the commonsense knowledge stored in zero-shot models. They need either complicated post-filter procedures or prompt template designs, and these tend to overlook contextual cues specific to the scene and lead to diverse undesired outcomes.

Orthogonal to these methods, we explore a new rearrangement routine, SG-Bot, that uses goal imagination on scene graphs and goal-guided object matching, as shown in Fig. 1. SG-Bot has three stages for the task: observation, imagination, and execution. In the first stage it processes the initial scenes and extracts objects with semantic instance segmentation. The imagination stage is coarse-to-fine. First the objects are treated as semantic nodes in a goal scene graph that we construct. The graph is directed either by commonsense reasoning or by user-defined rules, and it is the coarse goal state. For a finer generation, the goal scene graph can already be decoded into an actual scene with a scene generative model, Graph-to-3D. But because of the features of generative models, Graph-to-3D can produce diverse generation results that are inconsistent with the observation, and this can affect the precision of the object matching afterwards. We control the generation process by enriching the graph with shape priors to get a shape-aware graph, which has the initial shape knowledge. Then SG-Bot does finer goal scene imagination conditioned on this graph, so the imagined shapes are coherent with the initial observation. In the last stage, execution, the imagined objects are used as anchors to guide the object matching by point cloud registration during the scene transformation. At each transformation step we check occupancy between objects in the current observation and in the imagination so the rearrangement is safe.

SG-Bot is unique in three ways. First, compared to the goal-required methods, SG-Bot does not need known goal priors and can self-generate goal scenes just for the initial scenes. Second, compared to autoregressive methods, SG-Bot decouples the transformation policy by matching per object, which lowers the risk of error accumulation. Third, compared to the loose-coupled zero-shot methods, the concrete goal states and the closed-loop rearrangement strategy guarantee the rearrangement performance.

Our contributions are:

- • We present SG-Bot, a new paradigm for object rearrangement. The goal states are generated coarse-to-fine from rules represented as scene graphs, and goal-guided matching on them defines our motion policies.

- • We extract shape priors from the initial observation to alleviate ambiguous goal scene generation, and this improves rearrangement performance.

- • Experiments in simulation show that SG-Bot achieves competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods. The rearrangement performance also stays consistent in real-world scenarios.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Object rearrangement is an essential but challenging task in robot-environment interaction, marking a crucial capability in embodied AI [1]. This interactive ability reaches its highest level of automation by combining vision [2,3,4,5], textual insights from sources [6,7,8], and strategic motion planning [9,10]. Together, these elements result in a sophisticated physical embodiment for robots.

Robotic rearrangement refers to the process in which a robotic agent, starting from an initial configuration within a scene, re-positions objects according to specific rules or instructions. The purpose is to achieve desired goal states, relying solely on sensory data and onboard perceptions. Recently proposed vision-based solutions to this task can be categorized into three approaches: using known geometric and semantic goal states, sequential object pose estimation, and zero-shot rearrangement with large models. Typically, for goal-guided methods [11,12], the quality of such priors significantly affects the accuracy of the rearrangement, and when the goal state is unavailable, such methods cannot be applied in the real world. Moreover, for pose estimation based approaches [13], while the sequential design aligns well with robotic manipulations, it can suffer from cumulative errors in autoregressive predictions. The last type of methods [14,15,16,17,18] tap into commonsense knowledge stored in zero-shot models. They require either intricate post-filter procedures or prompt template designs, which tend to overlook scene-specific contextual cues and lead to diverse undesired outcomes.

Orthogonal to the above methodologies, we explore a novel rearrangement routine, SG-Bot, using goal imagination on scene graphs and goal-guided object matching, as shown in Fig. 1. SG-Bot stacks three stages for the task: observation, imagination, and execution. Specifically, in the first stage, it processes initial scenes to extract objects by semantic instance segmentation. The imagination stage follows a coarse-to-fine solution, where objects are first treated as semantic nodes in a constructed goal scene graph. This graph is directed either by commonsense reasoning or by user-defined rules, and serves as the coarse goal state. For a finer generation, the goal scene graph can already be decoded to an actual scene using a scene generative model, Graph-to-3D [19]. However, due to the features of generative models, Graph-to-3D can produce diverse generation results inconsistent with the observation, potentially affecting the precision of subsequent object matching. We control the generation process by enriching the graph with shape priors to obtain a shape-aware graph that carries the initial shape knowledge. Next, SG-Bot performs finer goal scene imagination conditioned on this graph, ensuring that the imagined shapes are coherent with the initial observation. Finally, in the execution stage, the imagined objects serve as anchors to guide object matching by point cloud registration during the scene transformation. At each transformation step, we check occupancy between objects in the current observation and the imagination for safe rearrangement. SG-Bot is unique in three aspects: First, compared to goal-required methods, e.g., [11,12], SG-Bot does not need known goal priors but can self-generate goal scenes exclusively for the initial scenes. Second, compared to autoregressive methods, e.g., [13], SG-Bot decouples the transformation policy using per-object matching to decrease the risk of error accumulation. Third, compared to loose-coupled zero-shot methods, e.g., [16], the concrete goal states and the closed-loop rearrangement strategy guarantee the rearrangement performance.

Our contributions are summarized as:

- • We present SG-Bot, a new paradigm for object rearrangement. The goal states are generated coarse-to-fine from rules represented as scene graphs, with which goal-guided matching defines our motion policies.

- • Ambiguous goal scene generation is alleviated by extracting shape priors from the initial observation, which improves rearrangement performance.

- • Experimental results in simulation show that SG-Bot achieves competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, the rearrangement performance remains consistent in real-world scenarios.
